newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU may extend Swedish quotas on alcohol until 2000.
newsitem.headline: EU may extend Swedish quotas on alcohol until 2000.

text.p: European Union finance ministers may agree next week to allow Sweden to extend its quotas on personal imports of alcohol and cigarettes until June 30, 2000, an EU source said on Thursday.

Sweden, saying its restrictions on personal alcohol imports are vital for its social and health policies, proposed at COREPER on Wednesday that its present rules should be extended to that date when they would be reviewed by the EU again.
In effect, this would mean that Sweden buys itself extra time as it would not already now have to agree to a final date on when the restrictions must end, which the Commission has demanded.
France indicated it could support the Swedish proposal while for example Germany and Britain would need to think it over before Monday's ECOFIN, when the issue is due to be settled.
The Swedish government has been lobbying intensively to win support for its position over the last few weeks and seems to have been successful, at least to some extent.
However, such a solution for Sweden would mean that the three Nordic countries would be treated differently.
Earlier this month, the Commission proposed that Denmark, Finland and Sweden phase out their limits on the amount of alcohol and cigarettes that travellers may bring home by June 30, 2002.
The EU executive has said the Nordic exemptions to EU rules, which allow them to restrict alcohol imports, were due to expire by the end of 1996 unless there was a new agreement.
Finland and Denmark have earlier indicated that they could accept the demand for fixing a final date for their quotas even if they would prefer it to be further away in time.

However, Swedish Finance Minister Erik Asbrink immediately threatened to veto the Commission proposal and indicated that Stockholm was prepared to defend itself in the EU court. Sweden refuses to agree a final date for ending its special rules.
A Finnish official said on Thursday that the situation would depend on what happens after June 30, 2000.
If it turns out that Sweden gets a more advantageous regime, then Finland and Denmark would want to be treated in the same way, he said.
Helsinki and Copenhagen therefore want ECOFIN to add a declaration to that effect on Monday.
The question of alcohol quotas is sensitive for the Nordic states, which have traditionally applied high taxes to alcohol and tobacco to discourage consumption and raise revenue.
Alcohol and tobacco taxes bring in about $2.7 billion annually in Sweden and $2.17 billion in Finland.
As Nordic excise duties on alcohol are much higher than elsewhere in the EU, some fear individual alcohol imports would jump if the Nordics lost their right to restrict the flow.
A Swede is currently allowed to take home one litre of spirits, five litres of wine and 15 litres of beer compared with 10, 90 and 110 litres respectively for other EU citizens.
